newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine traders say hearing China soyoil sales.
newsitem.headline: Argentine traders say hearing China soyoil sales.

text.p: The Chinese are in the market for South American soymeal but even more so for oil, Argentine traders said Thursday.
"It's been a cyclical thing, but we think they're buying again," a trader told Reuters, "They're looking more more oil than meal."
"We seem to be at levels where people expect volume to China," another trader said, "I don't know how much was traded but I assume business was done overnight."
Traders said Argentine soybean oil for July shipment was offered FOB at $530, while pellets were going for $230.

"The Chinese have been taking a lot more meal from South America this year than last," one trader said, "So far they've taken about 600,000 tonnes to 700,000 tonnes of meal and I'd say a million tonnes of oil."
Traders were divided about whether the relatively high price of Argentine soybeans was allowing local crushers much of a margin.

"I would say they're covering their variable costs. Crush margins basis August are seven to eight dollars a tonne," said one. But, while Argentine soybeans are being sold to crushers in Argentina, they are not attractive to for export.

"We cannot compete against Brazil, where the farmer selling has been much more aggressive on the nearbys," said a trader, who forecast Argentine exports of 1996/97 beans at just 450,000 tonnes, down from two million tonnes last season.
Spot Argentine FAS elevator soybeans were going for $282 Thursday.
Argentine soybean exports have also been hit by a big increase in local crushing capacity.

Traders said Argentine firm Vincentin bought two 30,000-tonne shipments of U.S. soybeans last week for November. But they stressed that Vincentin, which owns its own dock, can import more cheaply than other Argentine crushers.
Traders were skeptical about whether more U.S. beans would be bought.
One Argentine trader professed to be both astonished and grateful at Tuesday's big falls in U.S. soybeans after Cargill's announcement it was importing beans from Brazil.

"It's sometimes hard to believe how naive the U.S. funds are. We heard the Brazilians were selling to the U.S. ages ago," he said. "We were selling the inverse and they were taking it from us and finally they decide to exit and we can take our profits."
He added, "They only react when someone from Cargill confirms what everyone already knows. They were several traders which sold to the States, not just Cargill."
